deep.reconstruction:
The page is written rotated by 90° and is a loose scratch sheet. It holds pencil figures and short formula fragments. The figures are two circles, a large triangle with a curved arrow, a hatched triangle subdivided by a grid of lines with a vertex on a straight line, a circle and an ellipse/oval, and short line segments near the formulas. All of the formulas fit one topic: the 2D Laplacian, directional and normal derivatives, and the Green/Gauss boundary-integral identity in the plane. This is the potential-theory toolkit Riemann used from his 1851 dissertation onward. The next page is an excerpt from Poisson's work on terrestrial heat, so this is a working sheet on heat and potential theory.

Reconstruction (my ordering; the page itself is fragmentary):

(1) Rotated axes. Riemann writes x cos t + y sin t (the coordinate p along a direction at angle t). Implicitly (mine) p = x cos t + y sin t and q = -x sin t + y cos t.

(2) Directional / normal derivative. He writes ∂u/∂x cos t + ∂u/∂y sin t, and ∂u/∂n = ∂u/∂x cos(n,x) + ∂u/∂y cos(n,y). In other words ∂u/∂p = u_x cos t + u_y sin t. For a boundary curve with outward normal at angle t this is the normal derivative.

(3) Second derivatives in rotated coordinates. He writes ∂²u/∂p∂q = … and also forms the product ∂u/∂x·∂u/∂y. Filled in (mine):
- ∂²u/∂p² = u_xx cos²t + 2u_xy sin t cos t + u_yy sin²t
- ∂²u/∂q² = u_xx sin²t - 2u_xy sin t cos t + u_yy cos²t
- ∂²u/∂p∂q = (u_yy - u_xx) sin t cos t + u_xy (cos²t - sin²t)

Hence ∂²u/∂p² + ∂²u/∂q² = ∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y², the rotational invariance of the Laplacian, which is written on the page. The ∂u/∂x ∂u/∂y fragment probably belongs to the companion invariance (∂u/∂p)² + (∂u/∂q)² = (∂u/∂x)² + (∂u/∂y)², or to the off-diagonal term above.

(4) Boundary integral identity. Fragments: '∫ (∂u/∂x dy - ∂u/∂y dx)', '= ∫ ∂u/∂p dt', '∫(…)=0', and the circle with a boundary element ds marked. Together they express ∫∫_D (u_xx + u_yy) dx dy = ∮_∂D ∂u/∂n ds. Consequently ∮ ∂u/∂n ds = 0 for harmonic u. On a circle of radius r with x = r cos t, y = r sin t, the outward normal is the radial direction, so ∂u/∂n = u_x cos t + u_y sin t and ds = r dt. This explains why x cos t + y sin t (= r on the circle) appears.

(5) The hatched, gridded triangle and the triangle with an arrow look like a verification of the plane Green/Stokes identity by decomposing a region into small cells (or triangles). In that argument the interior edge contributions cancel and only the boundary integral survives. This is my interpretation of the drawing; no formulas are attached.
